title: Pipkin's Perfectly Practical Problems
markdown:
The lighthouse stood over a sparkling sea, a grand old guardian, and inside it lived Pipkin, an apprentice with a mind as neat as a tray of seashells and a heart that wanted to be helpful.

One extra-blustery Tuesday he decided the world could use his well-organized thoughts. For weeks, then months, he had pored over maps and charts, scribbling in the lantern-room, to make the Official Handbook for Enjoying the Seaside: every page the clearest, calmest, most precise instruction he could invent. One especially wise line: To avoid seaside troubles and ensure a fine visit, secure all loose things against the strong wind with a sailor’s knot, checked for perfect security. Another: For the best watching of the coast, keep a clear path for talking, free from anything that might distract. For quiet thought: Always watch for changes in the tide; let keen eyes discover the small shifts in the ocean’s rhythm. Tourists rushed the lighthouse and clutched the handbook as if it held a key. They quoted him aloud while sorting little seaside wobbles — a hat, a picnic cloth, a child who would not look at the horizon properly.

What the keeper’s manual never mentioned: well-meaning advice can be too helpful, and hilarious about it.

A bright afternoon brought a sudden fierce squall, a proper gale, a tantrum from a grumpy cloud that sent the sapphire water into a temper. Pipkin scrambled with all his might to secure the precious lighthouse lanterns, making sure not a single ray would be lost, busy until the storm packed its bags and moved on. The handbook had a chapter on gales. He did not have time to consult it, which later struck him as useful information.

Down in the rocky cove, Asha the alpaca — ears like velvet question marks — had woven herself into a retired fishing net while chatting to a piece of driftwood that was practically winking. “Oh dearie. The handbook must have advice.” She recalled: secure all loose things against the prevailing wind with a sailor’s knot, triple-checked. Loose things: check. Prevailing wind: check. She looked at the seaweed on her back. “I am quite loose. Trapped, that is.” She tied a long wet strand around a barnacle rock. Not a sailor’s knot. Not triple-checked. Secured, as secured as an alpaca in a net with seaweed can be.

Further along, Benji the bear cub was trying to warn gulls about a discarded sandwich near their sunning spot. Bouncy, honey-coloured, he wanted them to know, loudly. The gulls preferred the glint of sun. “Maintain a clear channel of communication!” He found a bleached whelk, put it to his lips, and bellowed, “THE SANDWICH IS HERE!” The flock startled into a flurry of white. Benji beamed. “A clear channel!” He had forgotten that clear often means understood.

Old Mr. Lake, hermit crab under a mossy stone, was bored. Tide far out, sun warm, nothing happening. He remembered: observe for tidal anomalies with unwavering focus. Anomalies were not his routine. He found a perfectly ordinary grey pebble. “This is as anomalous as it gets.” He stared for an hour, a crustacean statue of observation. No scuttle. No wiggle.

Pipkin, lanterns safe, came down expecting tea-talk and found Asha wrapped like a poorly made kelp doll, Benji triumphant with a shell and empty air, Mr. Lake locked in a gaze with geology.

Eyebrows climbed toward sandy hair. “What are you all doing?”

Asha rustled. “Securing loose things. Prevailing wind. As advised.”

Benji, shell still up: “Clear channel! Sandwich distribution!”

Mr. Lake pointed a claw. “Observing anomalies.”

A giggle arrived, then a laugh that bounced the sandy hair. “Literal friends. The handbook was meant to guide, not to be a star-map. Sometimes the best solution is not in the book. It is in thinking a little differently.”

He untangled Asha with a few deft tugs. He suggested Benji try a friendly audible shout next time, aimed at gulls rather than shell acoustics. He nudged Mr. Lake, who conceded, after more wiggles, that the pebble was ordinary.

Sunset painted the sky in orange, pink, and a lavender Pipkin had not put in the handbook. He brewed a pot of warming herbal tea, steam curling into the cool evening. Asha’s ears twitched contentedly over the cup, seaweed finally off her back. Benji, with a happy sigh, munched a crumbly biscuit and set the whelk down as if retiring an instrument. Mr. Lake offered a rare almost-smile as he lowered himself onto a smooth sun-warmed rock, pebble forgotten, tide beginning its ordinary return. They sorted themselves before the last ray disappeared, because Pipkin still liked a schedule, even after a day that had eaten one.

“A new chapter,” Pipkin said, eyes twinkling. “Creative Interpretations for Everyday Seaside Shenanigans. Honorary degrees all round.”

He logged squall-lanterns / seaweed knot / whelk-channel / pebble-stare in the handbook’s back margin in his neatest hand, left the net folded where nets belong, and let the tide do its own observing without a chapter heading. The lighthouse, still a guardian, had learned that practical problems sometimes require an impractical laugh, which Pipkin, neat as the prettiest shells, now filed under useful and did not try to triple-check.
